# Synthetic T-REX walking-cap examples

These deliberately tiny timetables demonstrate why an unrestricted arrival/boarding frontier cannot be filtered into a claimed complete capped frontier. They also distinguish a conservative certificate rejection from an objective mismatch.

Every identifier and timetable entry was authored for the examples. The fixtures contain no real transport feed, measured query trace, coordinates or operator identifiers. The fixed timezone and service date are model parameters, not evidence of a real service. `fixtures.json` is dedicated under CC0-1.0; see `LICENSE-CC0.txt`. The Go tests are separate MIT-licensed software.

The strict endpoint class has access/egress/direct limits of zero seconds, a transfer limit of 900 seconds, 900 aggregate walking seconds and two boardings. The other class has limits 600/600/900/900, 3900 aggregate walking seconds and four boardings. Both use zero transfer buffer, at most 1024 legs and query interval 26100–29700. Tests pass the original query unchanged.

| Fixture | Unchecked kernel representative | Literal feasible capped frontier |
|---|---|---|
| `access_hidden_alternative` | Walk 1 second before boarding; arrive 26300 with 1 boarding | Direct ride arrives 26400 with 1 boarding |
| `access_equal_objective_alternative` | Same infeasible access walk; arrive 26300 with 1 boarding | A different feasible ride has exactly the same (26300, 1) objective |
| `egress_hidden_alternative` | Walk 601 seconds after alighting; arrive 26901 with 1 boarding | Direct ride arrives 27000 with 1 boarding |
| `transfer_hidden_alternative` | Walk 901 seconds between rides; arrive 27400 with 2 boardings | A 900-second transfer produces arrival 27500 with 2 boardings |
| `direct_hidden_alternative` | Walk 901 seconds directly; arrive 27001 with 0 boardings | Ride arrives 27100 with 1 boarding |
| `accepted_without_walking` | Feasible ride arrives 26400 with 1 boarding | Same objective and witness; public certificate must complete mandatory verification |

The access examples each require only three stops, two rides and one walk. The equal-objective case deliberately names the access endpoint `A` and origin `Z`, selecting the infeasible tie representative first under the current deterministic ordering. It tests that behavior explicitly; it does not require every future tie policy to select this representative.

All fixtures except the supplementary direct-walk case use one partition level. The direct-walk case has one indivisible walking component, so it uses zero levels. It demonstrates cap handling without a rank cut between cells.

The public boundary rejects each infeasible unrestricted representative with empty output, `Complete=false` and `Accepted=false`. This is unsupported certification, never a complete no-route answer. Bounded independent enumeration finishes on each fixture and is compared against literal journey references and literal objective vectors. A separate checker replays every feasible witness. No expected answer is generated by T-REX or its pruning rules.

The separate kernel diagnostic uses an existing package-private entry point to inspect the witnesses the public certificate intentionally clears. It adds no production export. Raw objectives are descriptive and do not certify feasibility. Four hidden-alternative examples have capped objectives absent from the unrestricted frontier; the tie example instead has a feasible witness with the same objective. Filtering unchecked output alone resolves neither class.

Budget tests distinguish ranked-query work exhaustion, independent enumeration scan exhaustion, and objective-projection scan exhaustion. All must remain incomplete and clear output. An enumeration-complete flag is insufficient when the remaining projection budget is exhausted.

These are behavioral regressions and portable explanations, not performance benchmarks or a proof of general cap-aware rank preservation. A successful tiny suite does not establish bug freedom.
